title: Market Risk, Lesson 10: Risk decomposition - why the desks' VaRs sum to more than the bank's
subtitle: Marginal, incremental and component VaR - three different questions, three different numbers
whyItMatters: When capital has to be allocated or limits set desk by desk, the bank-wide VaR number does not divide. Choosing the wrong decomposition overcharges every desk and penalises precisely the desks delivering the largest diversification benefit.
openingQuestion: Adding up the standalone VaR of each trading desk usually gives a number larger than the VaR of the whole bank. Why?
openingOptions: Because each desk computes VaR at a different confidence level, so they cannot be added
Because the difference is exactly the diversification benefit between the desks
Because the bank-wide VaR leaves out some of the desks' smaller positions
Because the desks use different time horizons when computing VaR
explanation: The desks do not lose money on the same day. When the bond desk is down, the FX desk may be up, so the portfolio as a whole swings less than the sum of the swings of its parts. The gap between the sum of the standalone VaRs and the bank-wide VaR is exactly that diversification benefit. The practical problem is that the benefit has to be shared back out to the desks - set limits and capital charges on standalone VaR and every desk is overcharged, with the total charged far exceeding the bank's real risk.

diagram.label: The sum of the desks' standalone VaRs
Subtract the diversification benefit between desks
Equals the VaR of the whole bank
Component VaR shares that back out and sums exactly to the total

realWorldExample.description: A desk positioned against the rest of the bank can have a very large standalone VaR while its component VaR is close to zero, or even negative. Measuring it on standalone VaR forces that desk to cut its position, and the bank loses exactly the thing that was reducing its overall risk.

quiz.question: What is the core difference between component VaR and standalone VaR?
options: Component VaR uses a higher confidence level than standalone VaR
Component VaR is always larger than the same desk's standalone VaR
Component VaR only works for portfolios of under ten positions
Component VaR sums exactly to the VaR of the whole portfolio
quiz.explanation: That additivity is precisely the property that makes component VaR usable for allocation: the parts fit the whole exactly, so no piece of risk is double counted or dropped. Standalone VaRs sum to more than the whole by exactly the diversification benefit. Both measures are computed at the same confidence level on any number of positions, and component VaR is normally smaller than standalone - it can even be negative for a position that hedges the rest of the book.

quiz.question: What question does marginal VaR answer?
options: How much portfolio VaR changes if one more unit is added
How much portfolio VaR falls if the position is removed entirely
What percentage of the total VaR this position contributes
What this position's VaR would be if it stood entirely alone
quiz.explanation: Marginal VaR is the derivative of VaR with respect to the position weight - the effect of a small change. Removing the position outright is the question incremental VaR answers, and for a large position the two numbers differ substantially because the relationship is not linear. The share of total VaR is what component VaR reports, and the risk of the position in isolation is standalone VaR: four names, four distinct calculations, and confusing them is what makes limit debates circular.

quiz.question: Scenario: A desk has a standalone VaR of 80bn but a component VaR of only 10bn. What does that tell you?
options: The desk is computing VaR wrongly, since the two must match
The desk's positions largely offset the rest of the bank
That desk contributes the largest risk in the whole bank
The desk's position is too small to affect the total
quiz.explanation: The desk swings hard on its own but swings against the rest of the book, so its contribution to total risk is very small. Applying a limit based on the 80bn figure would force this desk to shrink and would raise the bank's risk rather than lower it. A small component VaR is not evidence of a small position - the standalone number rules that out - and the two figures are not supposed to match: they answer different questions.

quiz.question: Why is it wrong to charge capital to each desk on its standalone VaR?
options: Because the regulator bans standalone VaR for internal purposes
Because standalone VaR cannot be computed for a newly formed desk
Because the total charged far exceeds the bank's actual risk
Because standalone VaR understates each desk's real risk
quiz.explanation: The standalone VaRs sum to more than the bank-wide VaR, so charging on them is charging for a quantity of risk that does not exist. It also penalises hardest the desks delivering the largest diversification benefit - which is to say it creates exactly the wrong incentive. The direction of the error is upward rather than downward, no supervisor forbids the measure for internal use, and a new desk's standalone VaR is as computable as anyone else's.

quiz.question: How does incremental VaR differ from marginal VaR?
options: Incremental uses historical simulation, marginal uses the parametric method
Incremental applies only to new positions, marginal to existing ones
Incremental is stated in absolute value, marginal as a percentage
Incremental measures removing the position outright, marginal a small change
quiz.explanation: Marginal is a derivative, suited to decisions about small adjustments. Incremental compares two states, with and without the position, which suits a decision to accept or decline a whole trade. For a large position, extrapolating from the marginal figure gives the wrong answer because the relationship is not linear. Both can be computed under either simulation method and both are stated in currency, so neither the technique nor the unit separates them - the question being asked does.

practicePrompt.question: The bank-wide VaR is 300bn. The standalone VaRs of six desks sum to 480bn. What follows if capital is charged to each desk on its standalone VaR?
options: The desk that reduces total risk is penalised hardest, though it helps everyone
The charge is allocated fairly, since each desk pays for its own risk
The total charge still comes to exactly 300bn, only split differently
It cannot be measured, since a diversification benefit has no money value
practicePrompt.explanation: The 180bn gap between 480 and 300 is the diversification benefit, and charging on standalone VaR means splitting a 480bn bill for 300bn of real risk - the excess lands on somebody. The one who carries most of it is the desk with a large standalone VaR but a negative correlation to the rest of the book, which is exactly the desk PULLING DOWN the bank's total risk. Limits and capital charges then work against diversification itself. Component VaR exists to fix this: it sums exactly to 300bn, so each desk pays for what it contributes to the whole rather than for what it produces standing alone.

keyTakeaways: The standalone VaRs exceed the bank-wide VaR by exactly the diversification benefit between desks
Component VaR sums exactly to the total, which is what makes it usable for allocating capital and limits
Marginal VaR measures a small change; incremental VaR measures removing the position outright - two different questions
Charging capital on standalone VaR penalises hardest the desks that are reducing total risk

summary.keyIdea: Bank-wide VaR cannot be split by division. A correct split has to sum exactly to the total, or limits and capital charges end up working against diversification itself.

application.message: When you see risk limits set on each desk's standalone VaR, ask how the sum of those limits compares with the bank-wide VaR. The gap is the risk being counted twice.

sections.text: Adding up each desk's VaR always gives a number larger than the VaR of the whole bank. That is not an arithmetic error, and how the difference is handled decides whether limits are set right or wrong.
The difference has a name: diversification

The desks do not lose on the same day. The bond desk loses when rates rise; the FX desk gains or loses for other reasons. The portfolio therefore swings less than the sum of the parts, and that distance is the diversification benefit the bank gets from operating across several markets.

Standalone VaR asks how risky this desk is on its own. Marginal VaR asks how much the total changes if the position moves a little. Incremental VaR asks how much the total falls if the desk is removed entirely. Three different questions give three different numbers, and confusing them is a permanent source of argument when limits are allocated.
The only measure that sums exactly

Component VaR is constructed to have exactly one property: add up all the components and you get the VaR of the whole portfolio. That is what makes it usable for splitting capital and limits without double counting anything. A desk positioned against the rest of the book can have a component VaR near zero even though its standalone VaR is very large.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: Setting limits on standalone VaR squeezes hardest exactly the desks that are reducing total risk - the opposite of the incentive the bank wants.
Why the sum is larger, in numbers

Two trading desks, each with a VaR of 100. If their profits are perfectly correlated - a coefficient of 1 - the combined VaR is exactly 200 and there is no diversification benefit at all. With a correlation of 0.5, the combined VaR is the square root of (100² + 100² + 2 × 0.5 × 100 × 100), which is 173.2. With a correlation of 0, the figure is 141.4. The distance between 200 and the true combined VaR is the diversification benefit: 26.8 in the middle case, 58.6 in the last.

sections.label: Who does that 26.8 belong to
sections.text: This is the hard question, and it has no obvious answer. Neither desk creates that benefit on its own - it arises from the RELATIONSHIP between the two. Allocate it equally and a desk that is a natural hedge for the other gets no recognition for it. Allocate it on marginal VaR - how much total VaR falls when a desk is removed entirely - and the allocated parts usually do not sum to the amount being shared, so an adjustment is still needed. This is why risk decomposition is a governance problem rather than a division.

left.label: Limits set on each desk's standalone VaR
left.text: Simple and easy to explain, but it rewards each desk for reducing its own risk with no regard for the total portfolio. A desk that opens a hedging position for another desk sees its own VaR rise even though bank-wide risk falls - exactly the wrong incentive.

right.label: Limits set on contribution to total VaR
right.text: Harder to compute and harder to explain, but it measures the thing the bank actually cares about. A position that reduces total VaR gets a negative contribution, and the desk head is credited for the right thing they have just done.
